as a catalyst for much needed policy reform, generating both environmental, employment and economic gains [SEP] We are convinced that the current crisis can act as a catalyst for much needed policy reform, generating both environmental, employment and economic gains. [SEP] Goals: “It remains essential to deepen our work on new sources of growth, primarily on innovation and green growth. our capacity to innovate will improve our prospects for higher growth and productivity, while being instrumental in addressing the growing concerns around “scarcities”, including food, energy, water, land and environment. the implementation of the OECD Innovation Strategy will thus be of paramount importance in this context.” “Our culture of “policy sharing” could be combined to support a broader agenda for development, which would integrate mainstream OECD policy areas such as trade, investment, environmental sustainability, good governance, social progress, taxation, gender inequality and education. this agenda could also include tools to allow us to interact better with emerging and developing countries and to incorporate their perspectives into our work.” “We commit to ensuring that the economic recovery and future economic growth are consistent with sustainable development. We are convinced that the current crisis can act as a catalyst for much needed policy reform, generating both environmental, employment and economic gains. it is with this in mind that OECD members, as well as Chile, Estonia, Israel and Slovenia endorsed the Green Growth Declaration.” “[The Green Growth] Declaration welcomes OECD analytical contributions for an ambitious, effective, efficient and fair international agreement at the UN climate conference that will take place in Copenhagen at the end of this year, in accordance with the principle of common but differentiated responsibility and respective capabilities. It further welcomes the OECD work on the interface between long-term economic growth and the environment, as well as its analysis related to the economics of climate change and other environmental challenges.” “Not so long ago, ambitious environmental policies were believed to be affordable only when economies were growing strongly. Times have changed. Recovery from this global recession is being staked, in part, on the opportunity for ‘green growth’. Our work on policies to promote environmentally sustainable growth and to capture the economic opportunities offered by sustainable use of water, biodiversity and other natural resources is even more relevant for all stakeholders now.” “Innovation is a must for countries to advance on the path to sustainable growth and to address the major global and social challenges of our time. Now is no time for a u-turn on investments in innovation – governments must continue to nurture the key sources of long-term growth, or risk short-term gain for long-term pain. It’s not just about spending more – it’s about getting more bang for each tax dollar through policies that strengthen the links between the elements in the system of innovation and creative use of markets to “pull” on innovation. By implementing the OECD Innovation Strategy, governments can deliver more effective policies for innovation, and ensure that innovation makes life better for people around the world.” “The Trade Committee will strengthen its advocacy of opening markets further and continue to examine the impact of policy responses to the crisis and appropriate exit strategies, in collaboration with the WTO. Over the medium term, we place an especially high priority on developing a services trade restrictiveness index, which will greatly improve understanding of the impact of regulations on service sectors in OECD and major emerging economies. The relationships between trade and environment and trade and employment also warrant greater attention.” Problems: “For a number of years, there has been evidence of a growing gap between the messages conveyed by macro-economic statistics such as GDP and people’s perceptions about their own economic conditions. While this gap has already been evident for some time, it has been amplified by the financial and economic crises. this sentiment is damaging not only for the credibility of official statistics and public policies but for the very functioning of democracy.” “We shall resist protectionism. the free flow of trade and investment is essential to ensure a return to sustainable economic growth and improved standards of living for all, particularly for developing countries. We commit to openness, standstill, roll-back, and non-discrimination, to promote and facilitate global trade and investment, as endorsed by the 2 April 2009 London summit. the measures for assisting industries must be transparent, temporary and WTO consistent, minimising distortion on trade and investment.” (26-27) “The multilateral trading system was severely tested in 2009, but governments generally resisted protectionist pressures. Such pressures will persist in an environment where tight budgets and rising joblessness may prevail for some time. The timid economic recovery also adds to concerns about global food security, in particular for low income households in less developed countries. Now governments need not just to resist protectionism but to open markets further, in order to allow trade to contribute more to global economic growth, development and employment.”

efficient [SEP] We underline the importance of taking action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through rational and efficient use of energy and through other cost-effective means. [SEP] Policies: “To underscore our commitment to sustainable development we will step up our efforts to build a coherent global and environmentally responsive framework of multilateral agreements and institutions. We support the outcome of the G8 Environment Ministers' meeting in Schwerin and will expedite international cooperation on the establishment, general recognition and continual improvement of environmental standards and norms. We agree that environmental considerations should be taken fully into account in the upcoming round of WTO negotiations. This should include a clarification of the relationship between both multilateral environmental agreements and key environmental principles, and WTO rules.” “We agree to continue to support the Multilateral Development Banks in making environmental considerations an integral part of their activities and we will do likewise when providing our own support.” “We will therefore work towards timely progress in implementing the Buenos Aires Plan of Action with a view to early entry into force of the Kyoto Protocol. In particular, we encourage decisions on the operation of the Kyoto mechanisms and on a strong and effective compliance regime. We underline the importance of taking action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through rational and efficient use of energy and through other cost-effective means.”

consumption patterns [SEP] Environment and Employment work comprises three main components: an assessment of environmental policies in both past and present economic contexts; the employment implications of long-term trends or approaches in environmental management, in particular strategies aimed at promoting more sustainable production and consumption patterns. [SEP] OECD Annual Report 1993 Summary: Goals: “The ‘strategy’ [OECD Environmental Strategy for the 1990s] rests on three main ‘pillars’: integrating environment and economic decision-making; improving environmental performance (including the reduction of the pollution burden); and expanding international co-operation, both among OECD Members and through increased ‘outreach’ to other nations – notably the countries of central and eastern Europe, the newly independent states of the former Soviet Union and the dynamic economies in Asia and Latin America.” “By the end of 1993, the inter-committee working groups were active in the areas of trade and environment, agriculture and environment, tax policy and environment; and joint projects were underway on the environmental aspects of transport, energy and development co-operation.” “Other major trends in OECD’s environmental work which were extended during the year were: the shift from classical air, water and land pollution concerns to a focus on environmental policies in key economic sectors; the search for least-cost solutions to environmental policy; an emphasis on monitoring of compliance and evaluation of performance; strengthened partnerships with international and non-governmental institutions; and engagement of non-Member countries.” “The OECD continues to place a major emphasis on economic and environmental policy integration. One stream of work addresses policy instruments, including expanded use of market mechanisms, government regulations, voluntary agreements, pricing policy and institutional reform. A second stream addresses policy conflicts and integration of mechanisms in key economic sectors, while a third stream addresses the consequences of environmental policy changes for economic growth, employment and industry competitiveness, and the relationship between trade and environment issues.” “A major study was launched in 1993 which will assess the policies adopted by some countries to establish an environmentally-conscious pattern of urban development, and to provide guidelines to make cities more livable and more sustainable in the long run. In addition to benefits at the local level, cumulatively such policies will contribute to reducing global environmental problems and, perhaps at some point, change attitudes to the environment.” Problems: “Another feature of the Organisation’s evolving environmental work was an attempt to link it more tightly to major environmental issues and activities of a ‘global’ nature, to ensure that it supports the major international interests and needs of OECD Members.” “Environmental Indicators and Information work has focused in 1993 on constructing and testing indicators of environmental performance (an area of growing significance); measuring sectoral indicators to integrate environmental concerns in the agriculture, energy and transport sectors; and pilot activities on forest and water resources accounts which led to conclusions on natural resource accounting.” “A key finding of the Technology and Environment Programme was that, despite the existence of technologies which could achieve notable results in reducing pollution more cost-effectively, their penetration to date is slight and government role to stimulate the demand for such technologies is crucial.” “Work on the Environmental Aspects of Biotechnology concentrates on promoting harmonization of oversight/regulatory structures, seeking to avoid situations where regulatory uncertainties or differences might create unnecessary barriers to trade or technology diffusion; and on examining opportunities for biotechnology application to environmental improvements.” Policies: “Based on sectoral work, an analysis on how governments succeed in promoting policy integration and on the role of various factors which facilitate or impede policy integration is being carried out. [SEP] Summary The 2014 annual report continues to stress the link between poverty reduction, economic growth, and environmental sustainability, as with previous reports. It goes so far as to say that extreme poverty cannot be eliminated without first addressing key environmental issues such as climate change, and thus stresses the climate-barrier that can threaten to prevent progress in other realms of development. The Bank also stresses the importance to not only mitigate climate change for future effects, but to anticipate the unavoidable negative consequences of climate change. In the Bank’s efforts, it both works to mitigate and provide climate resilient frameworks for developing areas, so they are less vulnerable to climate issues later on. The Bank also establishes a new link to strengthen the relationship between environment and economic gains: it states that energy efficiency and greener energy pathways proves to improve both the environmental and economic landscapes, thus showing a positive correlation between the two. The Bank continued with climate specific initiatives in 2014, such as the Climate Investment Funds and the Bank’s Green Bond system. It also facilitated various forums between environmental stakeholders in a region capacity. It engages in both private and public partnerships to achieve climate gains. There was an increased emphasis on energy improvements and clean energy projects in the 2014 annual report, and the Bank justified these projects as a way to improve both environmental and economic well being. When delving into its various climate and environmental projects, the Bank continues to emphasize language that couples climate and economic pathways, such as “climate-smart growth” and other synonyms to green growth.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2016 Summary: The environment plays a major role in the OECD’s 2016 Annual Report. This includes the letter from the Secretary-General, the Strategic Orientations, the Ministerial Council Statement as well as other sections in the report. The introductory components of the report cite sustainable development as one of the foremost goals of the OECD. They reference the creation of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) which call for international cooperation and coordination in the development of economic policies that promote environmental sustainability while maintaining productivity growth. The OECD explicitly and repeatedly calls for green growth policies which include subsidy reform, carbon pricing, investment in green technology and infrastructure, possible environmental taxes and other economic tools. The OECD steadfastly maintains the importance and efficacy of multilateralism and calls for greater cooperation between International Organizations (IOs) in achieving green growth goals. The Key Activities section of the report contains three subsections devoted to environmental issues: Implementing the Green Growth Strategy, The Strategy on Development and Contribution to SDGs, and Aligning Policies for the Transition to a Low-Carbon Economy. This is in addition to the Environment and the Trade and Agriculture Directorates. Each of these sections call for policies that balance sustainability and growth. Through various policy subscriptions, the OECD repeats the need to look past short-term cost-benefit analyses and consider the long-term impacts of policy. Goals: “Our Organisation must work with others to develop a new growth narrative based around people’s well-being and environmental sustainability, and to help countries design, implement and monitor reforms to improve both productivity and inclusiveness.” “Advance major elements of the global agenda and support collective policy action. This includes efforts to leverage the installed capacity of the OECD to support the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement (COP21), as well as actively pursuing the implementation of the major agreements on tax in an inclusive manner to ensure that the existing loopholes in the international tax system are addressed effectively in the near term future.” “Examining the potential trade-offs and synergies of various policy objectives–equity, environment, productivity” “In addition, we should strengthen our national environmental assessments to help countries align their economic policies for a low-carbon economy. By integrating our work better with that of other IOs, we will try to capitalise on the current momentum in favour of more sustainable economic models.” “The Green Growth Strategy is driven by the premise – mandated by the June 2009 Ministerial Council Meeting – that “green” and “growth” must go hand-in-hand. It aims to support governments’ efforts to foster economic growth and development while ensuring that natural assets continue to provide the resources and environmental services on which our well-being relies. To help prevent costly environmental degradation and better manage natural resources, governments must catalyse investment and innovation in clean technologies and infrastructure. Such measures will help underpin sustained growth and give rise to new economic opportunities.” “New tools are being developed corresponding to the Sustainable Development Goals (SGDs) Target 17 to ‘enhance policy coherence for sustainable development,’ providing practical support to governments interested in adapting their institutional mechanisms and policy-making processes in a way that considers policy interactions, contextual factors and the effects of policies on well-being both now and in the future. These tools are works in progress and will include thematic modules on food security, illicit financial flows and green growth – the three priority areas for policy coherence identified by the Strategy.” “If the last 12 months were all about getting pen to paper, 2016 must centre on countries setting about implementation that gets the environment back on track. Great leadership has been shown to produce the Paris Climate Agreement and new SDGs [Sustainable Development Goals]. We will welcome many of these leaders back to Paris to the OECD Ministers’ Meeting in September where we’ll explore policies, tools and actions that work better for the economy and the environment.”

[SEP] UNDP Annual Report 2002 Summary: The 2002 UNDP Annual Report highlights the inclusion of environmental sustainability in the organization’s Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). The UNDP directly ties sustainable development to their notion of economic recovery. The report stresses the need for local governments to take action and promotes a decentralized vision of achieving sustainable development at the community level. To this end, the UNDP encourages the development of public-private partnerships as well as the engagement of civil society organizations to produce innovative policies. They also point to volunteerism as a key aspect of achieving the MDGs. The report recognizes the challenges posed by the lack of financial and political support and calls for a remobilization of these assets. Furthermore, the UNDP sees international coordination as the only way to sufficiently address truly global environmental problems (e.g. climate change, biodiversity loss, ozone depletion). They also recognize that the poor are the most adversely affected by environmental degradation, thus rendering the need for international cooperation even more urgent. Green Economy [SEP] The UNEP claims that its Global Green New Deal and Green Economy initiative translate sustainable development into an actionable agenda, putting the environment at the center of global affairs. [SEP] Summary The UNEP’s 2008 Annual Report reiterates the value in pursuing a green economy based on efficient and equitable resources. The UNEP says that not only will this cut down greenhouse gas emissions and protect essential ecosystems, but also reinvigorate national economies, improve human well-being and achieve the targets of the international community. This report further describes the goals of the UNEP under the Green New Deal to combat climate change and address the many interlinked environmental and development challenges. The UNEP claims that its Global Green New Deal and Green Economy initiative translate sustainable development into an actionable agenda, putting the environment at the center of global affairs. As such, throughout the report they focus on the cost cutting initiatives that would allow for more prosperous national economies while simultaneously working to reduce the harmful impacts of climate change in areas such as energy and fossil fuel consumption. Through the Green Economy Initiative, the UNEP plans to draw on the existing work of the UN and UNEP, ranging from impacts and opportunities of shifting fish, fuel and other subsidies, up to innovative market mechanisms and financials products that have already initiated the transition. UNEP expects investors to dispatch trillions of dollars back into the market during 2009 or 2010, and urges that this needs to flow into the new Green Economy, not the one of the past that left a harmful ecological footprint. It believes that this will be a fresh way of getting public and private finance to focus on what matters in regards to climate change. They believe it will help deliver a more intelligent, resource-efficient, environmentally responsible and socially equitable development path that is inclusive of all economies and peoples.

[SEP] Summary In 2017, the bank continued to draw links between economic growth, environmental sustainability, and poverty reduction, and emphasized how these three components are integral in creating sustainable development. It highlighted the importance of increasing climate financing. The Bank also stressed how climate change disproportionately affects the most impoverished citizens who are the least economically stable. It views low-carbon development as something that produces a positive feedback loop too: not only does green economic growth contribute to development but this development in turn provides more potential for climate action that generates job creation and economic growth. The 2017 report continued to expand on past environmental and climate initiatives of the past few years. It also began to describe more projects addressing new subsets of environmentally related interests. For example, it addresses the importance of green growth through transportation technology, in the form of increased energy efficiency and low-carbon technological development strategies. It also worked towards greening the financial sector with benchmark bonds and World Bank Green Bonds, which go on to finance environmentally sustainable and renewable energy projects. The Bank continued to increase its carbon emissions transparency and green project transparency by having partners and NGOs assess their work. The Bank also continued with projects that addressed climate related weather risk and damages, in addition to mitigation projects.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2010 Summary: The 2010 OECD Annual Report suggests a strong linkage between economic growth and environmental sustainability. The OECD goes as far as to argue that that recovery from the global financial crisis is being “staked” on green growth. In this sense, green growth provides an opportunity both to restore growth lost during the crash and to respond to global environmental crises (some of which were precipitated by the very actions that led to the financial crisis).The OECD also calls for a recognition that traditional metrics of growth (e.g. GDP) often do not reflect fully the well-being of a nation. We need to develop additional indicators of sustainability to fully understand the state of the global economy. The OECD points to the carbon tax and emissions-trading as concrete policies which can simultaneously create revenue for governments and help reduce GHG emissions. Innovation in green technology and infrastructure are also key to the OECD’s vision of green growth. This innovation must be supported through public and private investment. Continued multilateral negotiations on climate change are essential and any unilateral action should be discouraged. The OECD sees no alternative to the liberal order as far as establishing a green economy is concerned.

The OECD’s Green Growth Strategy claims that not only that “green” and “growth” can go together, but that they must. The OECD asserts that achieving green growth goals must be the result of coordinated international and institutional cooperation. To this end, the OECD attempts to discredit protectionism and suggests that a multilateral approach must be taken to achieve sustainable development goals. Investment and innovation are central to the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy. They also emphasize the need to better understand the long-term economic cost of inaction in the face of environmental crises and, conversely, the long-term economic benefit of positive action. This is as opposed to simply considering short-term costs and benefits which do not fully reflect the consequences of action or inaction. This analysis includes developing new indicators for growth and strengthening our statistical capacities to interpret such data. Green technology and infrastructure are central to a modern green economy. Once environmental assets and natural resources are valued properly, countries will begin to see that it is in their economic interest to protect the environment.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2015 Summary: The OECD’s 2015 Annual Report highlights the work of the OECD in the move towards sustainable development, through what they call green growth policies. They assert that there is no tradeoff between environmental protection and economic growth--in fact, they suggest that the two go hand-in-hand. The Strategic Orientations of the Secretary-General lay out the OECD’s desire for a transition to a low-carbon global economy which, in their words, will offer sustainability and resilience in the face of crisis like climate change. A section of the report is dedicated to the Ministerial Council Statement regarding Climate Change. Here, the council reaffirms the need for coordinated international cooperation (e.g. OECD, IEA, NEA, ITF, UNFCCC) in the transition to a low-carbon economy. Through international institutional alignment and cooperation, the OECD believes that national governments will have clear indicators as to the future trajectory of global economy. The Ministerial Council statement lays out a variety of policy proposals to achieve their goal. These include investment in technological R&D, investment in infrastructure, subsidy reform, and strengthening international trade to name a few. In the Key Activities section of the Report, the OECD mentions their continued development of the Green Growth Strategy, which is a staple of their Annual Reports. Here, the OECD again makes clear that governments can foster economic growth while protecting national environments. Per usual, the report also includes sections pertaining to the work of the Environment and the Trade and Agriculture Directorates. The Environment Directorate reiterates the OECD’s work in promoting investment in green technology and infrastructure. The Trade and Agriculture Directorate mentions agriculture (e.g. fisheries) as a sector of the economy which is especially conducive to the simultaneous improvements in sustainability and productivity. Multilateral trade can help ensure that suppliers meet demand while maintaining sustainable resource use. [SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2012 Summary: The 2012 OECD Annual Report stresses the fact that economic growth and environmental sustainability do not constitute a “zero sum game.” That is to say, an improvement in one does not necessarily detract from the other. In fact, the OECD claims that the two go hand-in-hand. In light of the global financial crisis, the OECD recognizes the need to rebuild national economies and restore global growth. In doing so, however, productivity cannot be the only metric we take into account as far as growth is concerned--we must also consider equity and sustainability. Technological innovation, which is achieved through investment, is key to the greening of the global economy. To foster a productive, sustainable, and equitable global economy, the OECD points to the development of their Green Growth Strategy and Rio+20 as examples of efficacious international cooperation. Multilateralism is the way of the future for the OECD. Accordingly, they argue that protectionism and beggar-thy-neighbor policies are impediments to creating sustainable development. Liberal multilateral trade must underpin any effort to green the global economy. Education, skills training, and knowledge sharing are all identified as critical undertakings for the OECD. Efforts will also be bolstered by the proper valuation of environmental assets.

[SEP] Summary The World Bank annual report for 2000 strongly emphasized the link between poverty reduction and environmental progress. The report also describes environmental problems as constraints that threaten the potential for economic growth. The report interlinks the topics of poverty, economic growth, and environmental sustainability by describing the impoverished as individuals most vulnerable to economic issues, and environmental problems as a barrier to overcome economic issues in order to produce economic growth. In 2000, the World Bank continued to assist with the implementation of financing for environmental projects through both the Global Environment facility (GEF) and the Multilateral Fund of the Montreal Protocol (MFMP). In addition to lending mechanisms, the Bank also emphasized the importance of nonlending efforts, such as analytical studies with local communities of national governments around a variety of environmental protection issues. The Bank also worked to remove environmentally related investor risks as well as develop better legal proceeding to regulate environmental degradation/remediation issues. The World Bank continued to support and assist with the implementation and design for national environmental plans. However, in 2000 the Bank also began to emphasize the importance of empowering local citizens and governments to begin carrying on World Bank initiatives independently at a certain point after initial set up. The Bank also established the Prototype Carbon Fund in 2000, to directly tackle issues of climate change and emissions reductions in partner countries, by facilitating the transfer of climate-friendly technology to developing countries.

In order to keep the costs of action low, market-based instruments such as carbon taxes or emissions trading schemes should be prominent in the mix. These instruments can help to put a “price” on greenhouse gas emissions that is the same across sectors, gases, and countries. This would minimise the total cost, ensure mitigation action takes place where it is most efficient, and provide an incentive for further technological innovation. Linking existing emissions trading schemes, and strengthening and scaling up the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), can help to contribute to a global carbon market.” But market-based instruments will need to be complemented by other policy instruments, such as regulations and standards, support for R&D into climate-friendly technologies, information-based instruments (e.g. fuel efficiency labels for vehicles), and voluntary approaches. [SEP] Summary In 2017, the bank continued to draw links between economic growth, environmental sustainability, and poverty reduction, and emphasized how these three components are integral in creating sustainable development. It highlighted the importance of increasing climate financing. The Bank also stressed how climate change disproportionately affects the most impoverished citizens who are the least economically stable. It views low-carbon development as something that produces a positive feedback loop too: not only does green economic growth contribute to development but this development in turn provides more potential for climate action that generates job creation and economic growth. The 2017 report continued to expand on past environmental and climate initiatives of the past few years. It also began to describe more projects addressing new subsets of environmentally related interests. For example, it addresses the importance of green growth through transportation technology, in the form of increased energy efficiency and low-carbon technological development strategies. It also worked towards greening the financial sector with benchmark bonds and World Bank Green Bonds, which go on to finance environmentally sustainable and renewable energy projects. The Bank continued to increase its carbon emissions transparency and green project transparency by having partners and NGOs assess their work. The Bank also continued with projects that addressed climate related weather risk and damages, in addition to mitigation projects.

“green” and “growth” [SEP] The OECD’s Green Growth Strategy claims that not only that “green” and “growth” can go together, but that they must. [SEP] Summary: The 2013 OECD Annual Report outlines the OECD’s commitment to green growth policies. The OECD states that equality and sustainability must be at the center of economic growth, suggesting that while productivity is still key it is no longer the be all end all of growth. The OECD’s Green Growth Strategy claims that not only that “green” and “growth” can go together, but that they must. The OECD asserts that achieving green growth goals must be the result of coordinated international and institutional cooperation. To this end, the OECD attempts to discredit protectionism and suggests that a multilateral approach must be taken to achieve sustainable development goals. Investment and innovation are central to the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy. They also emphasize the need to better understand the long-term economic cost of inaction in the face of environmental crises and, conversely, the long-term economic benefit of positive action. This is as opposed to simply considering short-term costs and benefits which do not fully reflect the consequences of action or inaction. This analysis includes developing new indicators for growth and strengthening our statistical capacities to interpret such data. Green technology and infrastructure are central to a modern green economy. Once environmental assets and natural resources are valued properly, countries will begin to see that it is in their economic interest to protect the environment.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2011 Summary: The environment plays a major role in the OECD’s 2011 Annual Report. They argue that the recovery from the global financial crisis must be undertaken with not only productivity in mind, but also sustainability and equity. For the OECD, economic growth and environmental protection are not opposing forces. Instead, the global economy can foster growth while preserving the environment. The OECD stresses the need to pay equal weight to the economic consequences of environmental policies and the environmental consequences of economic policies. At the heart of the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy is innovation: innovation in green technology and infrastructure. In the wake of the financial crisis, however, public and private investment has plateaued. The OECD calls for a revitalization of investment, both public and private. Increased investment in concert with more traditional measures like subsidy reform, environmental taxes, and emissions trading can lead to significant environmental protection while fostering economic growth. In its role as an international institution, the OECD warns against protectionism and unilateral action. Liberal trade and multilateralism (international and institutional) are at the core of the OECD’s mission and strategy. Goals: “Simply returning to growth will not be sufficient. We must draw all possible lessons from the crisis. We need to do so against a background of climate change, high unemployment levels, particularly among the youth, increasing inequalities, large fiscal deficits and very high debt accumulation. The economic growth model we should champion must take into account the impact on the environment, its redistributive capacity and the international linkages, via trade, investment and migration.” “Indeed, growth remains the key driver for employment and wealth creation. Fair and open markets, competition and innovation are all critical to growth. But we also need a more inclusive and greener model of growth based on sound institutions. Searching for new sources of growth that are also “green”, more equitable and more “gender friendly” has become our common objective to overcome the effects of the crisis.” “These strategic orientations reach beyond the need to find new sources of growth and explore policies to address the employment, social, environmental, and development aspects. The OECD @ 50 is an organisation that strives to improve the prospects of growth and welfare in member and partner countries, that encourages civic participation and equality of opportunities, and that seeks to realign the economy with the environment.” “With about 3% of OECD countries’ potential output lost as a result of the crisis, the time has come for the OECD to develop bold new thinking to address changing economic realities. New sources of balanced, sustainable and equitable growth are necessary. Identifying these new sources of growth and tapping into their full potential is one of our key priorities. Structural reforms will be critical to help enhance the productive capacity of our economies, foster employment, unleash investment and address issues of inclusiveness and social cohesion, so that the benefits of sustained growth are shared equitably.” “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. The OECD’s strategic approach contains much more than growth and recovery – this strategic approach reflects the “stronger”, “cleaner” and “fairer” aspects of our vision and it focuses on our mission of achieving “better policies for better lives” for our citizens.” “The pillars of our substantive focus include macroeconomic policies and financial markets, green growth, innovation, climate change and water, education, employment and skills, social policies, gender equality, migration, governance, anti-corruption and integrity, trade and investment, the OECD Better Life Initiative and a broader OECD development strategy which includes innovation, investment, domestic resource mobilisation, food security, measurement and knowledge sharing.” “Building on the successful results of the COP 16 United Nations Conference on Climate Change in Cancún, we will strengthen our work on climate change, in particular to help countries develop effective and least-cost policy mixes to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In our work on climate change, fossil fuel subsidies and energy-related issues, we will continue to work with the IEA.” “If we can foster a real cross-fertilisation of ideas, it will help us to stay at the frontier of new thinking and ensure we provide relevant and pragmatic advice to governments in their efforts to design and implement better policies for better lives. We also need to continue to produce norms and standards which by their quality and credibility can be embraced by the international community.” Problems: “The world economy is still going through difficult times. The global crisis has left several countries with a legacy of low growth, high unemployment, unsound public finances and lower potential output. Although recovery is underway, it is unbalanced across countries and regions. In most of the emerging economies, high inflation driven by commodity and oil prices is a major concern.” “The food crisis affects all, particularly the poor. Recent natural catastrophes have drawn even more attention to questions about climate change and energy for the future. We are in the midst of a governance upheaval in the MENA [Middle East and North Africa] region, the full implications of which are still unknown. We do know, however, that poverty, income gaps, high unemployment, food insecurity, lack of education and gender inequality all matter for governance outcomes. These challenges call for strong and collective action. The OECD will contribute with well-developed forms of co-operation and engagement.” “Advanced, emerging and developing countries will face different challenges and opportunities, as will countries with differing economic and political circumstances. There are, on the other hand, common considerations that need to be addressed in all settings. Making green growth work, implementing the strategy and supporting member and partner countries in their policies for a greener growth path will figure among OECD’s top strategic priorities for the next few years.” “Poverty prevents most of the world’s hungry population from accessing food. This becomes a vicious circle, as food insecurity then threatens social cohesion and political stability; and not just in the region most immediately affected by supply shortfalls. The recent hikes in food prices have only aggravated this longstanding problem.” “We need to continue to show that there is added value in multilateral co-operation rather than acting unilaterally. We also need to strengthen our co-operation with other international organisations. We proposed the creation of a network for co-operation on policy coherence, bringing together the international organisations involved in the G20 (IMF, World Bank, FSB, ILO, WTO and OECD). The objective would be to improve co-ordination and exchange of information among international organisations.” “One key challenge in the past year has been finding a way to make the case for green growth. Governments have made it clear that unless they can deliver economic growth at the same time as meeting environmental challenges, they stand little chance of implementing ambitious new policies. We need to be equally concerned about the environmental impact of economic policies and the economic impact of environmental policies. The Green Growth project will operationalise that for the first time.” Policies: “The OECD Green Growth Strategy, to be launched at this year’s Ministerial, aims to develop an actionable policy framework with specific tools and recommendations in a broad range of areas, including fiscal, innovation, trade, labour and social policies to help governments achieve the most efficient shift to greener growth. Innovation will play a key role in this shift. Greening the growth path of an economy depends on policy and institutional settings, level of development, resource endowments and particular environmental pressure points.” “Our pioneering work on a comprehensive policy mix, including the use of economic instruments such as taxes and emission trading schemes, provides the main tools needed in the fight against climate change. There is already evidence of leading companies shifting to a low-carbon business model, starting with measuring their greenhouse gas emissions and then taking action to reduce them, and the OECD will continue to examine the policies and conditions that can best incentivise private sector action.” “Considering the recent accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, we should work through the NEA on strengthening safety standards for both existing and future plants and ensuring that all the lessons from this accident are incorporated. This would help alleviate public concerns and allow nuclear power to continue to play an important role in the global energy mix and in the fight against climate change.” “We will build on the OECD’s role as the premier forum for monitoring international public finance flows, to develop systems for better tracking private financing and to assess the options for scaling-up financing for climate change. We will also continue our strong commitment to providing policy guidance on improving water policy through our work on the economic, institutional and policy responses to the water challenge.” “Improving agricultural productivity and the functioning of local and global agricultural markets as well as the liberalisation of trade are essential. But durable solutions will also feature improvements in systems of governance and the overall business environment in developing countries and increased investments in health, education and physical infrastructure.” “We will continue to support the G20 on the following priorities: on the adoption of structural policies within the Framework for Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth; on policies for employment, skills and jobs; on policies to liberalise trade, investment and capital flows; on the promotion and adoption of standards for anti-corruption; on the abolishment of fossil fuel subsidies; on policies for efficient, fair and transparent taxation systems; on food security and commodity markets; and on the Seoul Consensus for Shared Growth and its Multi-Year-Action Plan.” “There is a good reason why ‘innovation’ is one of today’s most common buzzwords in public policy. It is an important method for fuelling economic growth and addressing urgent social challenges like climate change and ageing societies. Stimulating innovation is not about spending money – it is about better co-ordination, long-term policy commitment, breaking down barriers and meeting people’s needs. Through its work on innovation, science, technology and industry, the OECD strives to deliver the most effective policy recommendations on key emerging issues facing governments.” “Rising commodity prices are again having a devastating impact on low income households around the world; immediate humanitarian relief is needed. But governments must also act to address the fundamental cause of global food insecurity: poverty. This means improving systems of governance and the overall business environment in less developed economies, to encourage widespread growth and employment; increasing public and private investment in developing country agriculture, in particular to increase productivity; and opening agricultural markets so that products can flow from surplus to deficit areas.”

green growth [SEP] “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. [SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2011 Summary: The environment plays a major role in the OECD’s 2011 Annual Report. They argue that the recovery from the global financial crisis must be undertaken with not only productivity in mind, but also sustainability and equity. For the OECD, economic growth and environmental protection are not opposing forces. Instead, the global economy can foster growth while preserving the environment. The OECD stresses the need to pay equal weight to the economic consequences of environmental policies and the environmental consequences of economic policies. At the heart of the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy is innovation: innovation in green technology and infrastructure. In the wake of the financial crisis, however, public and private investment has plateaued. The OECD calls for a revitalization of investment, both public and private. Increased investment in concert with more traditional measures like subsidy reform, environmental taxes, and emissions trading can lead to significant environmental protection while fostering economic growth. In its role as an international institution, the OECD warns against protectionism and unilateral action. Liberal trade and multilateralism (international and institutional) are at the core of the OECD’s mission and strategy. Goals: “Simply returning to growth will not be sufficient. We must draw all possible lessons from the crisis. We need to do so against a background of climate change, high unemployment levels, particularly among the youth, increasing inequalities, large fiscal deficits and very high debt accumulation. The economic growth model we should champion must take into account the impact on the environment, its redistributive capacity and the international linkages, via trade, investment and migration.” “Indeed, growth remains the key driver for employment and wealth creation. Fair and open markets, competition and innovation are all critical to growth. But we also need a more inclusive and greener model of growth based on sound institutions. Searching for new sources of growth that are also “green”, more equitable and more “gender friendly” has become our common objective to overcome the effects of the crisis.” “These strategic orientations reach beyond the need to find new sources of growth and explore policies to address the employment, social, environmental, and development aspects. The OECD @ 50 is an organisation that strives to improve the prospects of growth and welfare in member and partner countries, that encourages civic participation and equality of opportunities, and that seeks to realign the economy with the environment.” “With about 3% of OECD countries’ potential output lost as a result of the crisis, the time has come for the OECD to develop bold new thinking to address changing economic realities. New sources of balanced, sustainable and equitable growth are necessary. Identifying these new sources of growth and tapping into their full potential is one of our key priorities. Structural reforms will be critical to help enhance the productive capacity of our economies, foster employment, unleash investment and address issues of inclusiveness and social cohesion, so that the benefits of sustained growth are shared equitably.” “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. The OECD’s strategic approach contains much more than growth and recovery – this strategic approach reflects the “stronger”, “cleaner” and “fairer” aspects of our vision and it focuses on our mission of achieving “better policies for better lives” for our citizens.” “The pillars of our substantive focus include macroeconomic policies and financial markets, green growth, innovation, climate change and water, education, employment and skills, social policies, gender equality, migration, governance, anti-corruption and integrity, trade and investment, the OECD Better Life Initiative and a broader OECD development strategy which includes innovation, investment, domestic resource mobilisation, food security, measurement and knowledge sharing.” “Building on the successful results of the COP 16 United Nations Conference on Climate Change in Cancún, we will strengthen our work on climate change, in particular to help countries develop effective and least-cost policy mixes to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In our work on climate change, fossil fuel subsidies and energy-related issues, we will continue to work with the IEA.” “If we can foster a real cross-fertilisation of ideas, it will help us to stay at the frontier of new thinking and ensure we provide relevant and pragmatic advice to governments in their efforts to design and implement better policies for better lives. We also need to continue to produce norms and standards which by their quality and credibility can be embraced by the international community.” Problems: “The world economy is still going through difficult times. The global crisis has left several countries with a legacy of low growth, high unemployment, unsound public finances and lower potential output. Although recovery is underway, it is unbalanced across countries and regions. In most of the emerging economies, high inflation driven by commodity and oil prices is a major concern.” “The food crisis affects all, particularly the poor. Recent natural catastrophes have drawn even more attention to questions about climate change and energy for the future. We are in the midst of a governance upheaval in the MENA [Middle East and North Africa] region, the full implications of which are still unknown. We do know, however, that poverty, income gaps, high unemployment, food insecurity, lack of education and gender inequality all matter for governance outcomes. These challenges call for strong and collective action. The OECD will contribute with well-developed forms of co-operation and engagement.” “Advanced, emerging and developing countries will face different challenges and opportunities, as will countries with differing economic and political circumstances. There are, on the other hand, common considerations that need to be addressed in all settings. Making green growth work, implementing the strategy and supporting member and partner countries in their policies for a greener growth path will figure among OECD’s top strategic priorities for the next few years.” “Poverty prevents most of the world’s hungry population from accessing food. This becomes a vicious circle, as food insecurity then threatens social cohesion and political stability; and not just in the region most immediately affected by supply shortfalls. The recent hikes in food prices have only aggravated this longstanding problem.” “We need to continue to show that there is added value in multilateral co-operation rather than acting unilaterally. We also need to strengthen our co-operation with other international organisations. We proposed the creation of a network for co-operation on policy coherence, bringing together the international organisations involved in the G20 (IMF, World Bank, FSB, ILO, WTO and OECD). The objective would be to improve co-ordination and exchange of information among international organisations.” “One key challenge in the past year has been finding a way to make the case for green growth. Governments have made it clear that unless they can deliver economic growth at the same time as meeting environmental challenges, they stand little chance of implementing ambitious new policies. We need to be equally concerned about the environmental impact of economic policies and the economic impact of environmental policies. The Green Growth project will operationalise that for the first time.” Policies: “The OECD Green Growth Strategy, to be launched at this year’s Ministerial, aims to develop an actionable policy framework with specific tools and recommendations in a broad range of areas, including fiscal, innovation, trade, labour and social policies to help governments achieve the most efficient shift to greener growth. Innovation will play a key role in this shift. Greening the growth path of an economy depends on policy and institutional settings, level of development, resource endowments and particular environmental pressure points.” “Our pioneering work on a comprehensive policy mix, including the use of economic instruments such as taxes and emission trading schemes, provides the main tools needed in the fight against climate change. There is already evidence of leading companies shifting to a low-carbon business model, starting with measuring their greenhouse gas emissions and then taking action to reduce them, and the OECD will continue to examine the policies and conditions that can best incentivise private sector action.” “Considering the recent accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, we should work through the NEA on strengthening safety standards for both existing and future plants and ensuring that all the lessons from this accident are incorporated. This would help alleviate public concerns and allow nuclear power to continue to play an important role in the global energy mix and in the fight against climate change.” “We will build on the OECD’s role as the premier forum for monitoring international public finance flows, to develop systems for better tracking private financing and to assess the options for scaling-up financing for climate change. We will also continue our strong commitment to providing policy guidance on improving water policy through our work on the economic, institutional and policy responses to the water challenge.” “Improving agricultural productivity and the functioning of local and global agricultural markets as well as the liberalisation of trade are essential. But durable solutions will also feature improvements in systems of governance and the overall business environment in developing countries and increased investments in health, education and physical infrastructure.” “We will continue to support the G20 on the following priorities: on the adoption of structural policies within the Framework for Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth; on policies for employment, skills and jobs; on policies to liberalise trade, investment and capital flows; on the promotion and adoption of standards for anti-corruption; on the abolishment of fossil fuel subsidies; on policies for efficient, fair and transparent taxation systems; on food security and commodity markets; and on the Seoul Consensus for Shared Growth and its Multi-Year-Action Plan.” “There is a good reason why ‘innovation’ is one of today’s most common buzzwords in public policy. It is an important method for fuelling economic growth and addressing urgent social challenges like climate change and ageing societies. Stimulating innovation is not about spending money – it is about better co-ordination, long-term policy commitment, breaking down barriers and meeting people’s needs. Through its work on innovation, science, technology and industry, the OECD strives to deliver the most effective policy recommendations on key emerging issues facing governments.” “Rising commodity prices are again having a devastating impact on low income households around the world; immediate humanitarian relief is needed. But governments must also act to address the fundamental cause of global food insecurity: poverty. This means improving systems of governance and the overall business environment in less developed economies, to encourage widespread growth and employment; increasing public and private investment in developing country agriculture, in particular to increase productivity; and opening agricultural markets so that products can flow from surplus to deficit areas.”

[SEP] Summary The 2015 World Bank annual report continues to express strong links between, poverty reduction, development, and environmental sustainability (with an emphasis on climate-specific environmental sustainability). The report urges for an environmentally clean and climate-friendly development pathway. It also articulates the disproportionate threat on the poorest world citizens of natural disasters caused by climate change; addressing climate change is both seen as looking for emission reduction development methods as well as safeguarding communities against increased climate risks that are predicted to occur. In a different strain of thought, the World Bank stresses the link between the biodiversity/sustainability of ecosystems and the potential for economic growth. The World Bank suggests that we can continue trends of economic growth by sustaining and safeguarding natural capital for the future. In terms of environmental initiatives and climate policies, the World Bank 2015 annual report emphasizes a variety of projects, most of which are well established initiatives spanning from years prior. Examples include the Green Bonds program, the Global Environment Facility (GEF) grant management, and corporate social responsibility regarding environmental impact in the World Bank operations internally. This report also gave a renewed emphasis on climate-smart agricultural practices and technologies, climate-friendly transportation systems, and energy efficiency/renewability initiatives. Additionally, the Bank discussed work with developing carbon pricing and expanding accessible research knowledge on climate change and its implications. Notably, 2015 marks the transition year between the closure of the Millenium Development Goals and the commencement of adopting the Sustainable Development Goals.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2014 Summary: The OECD’s 2014 Annual Report reiterates themes from recent (past and future) reports regarding environmental sustainability. The Secretary-General’s Strategic Orientation affirm green growth as one of the, if not the, primary goal of the institution. The report goes so far as to say that the green growth framework must “permeate” all levels of the institution and its work. Green growth for the OECD means the creation of coherent policies which promotes economic productivity and environmental sustainability together. The OECD Strategy on Development identifies diminishing multilateral cooperation and stagnant investment as primary obstacles to sustainable development. To correct these failures, the OECD stresses the importance of international and institutional cooperation. The section on the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy lays out general ideas and some specific policy proposals for achieving sustainable and resilient growth. These include investment in technology and infrastructure, effective tax policy (e.g. carbon pricing), subsidy reform, and broader work towards better understanding the synergies between the economy and the environment. The Environment Directorate recognizes the challenges of quantifying the long-term economic impact of environmental degradation and recognizes the need for continued work in this field. The Trade and Agriculture Directorate identifies protectionism and localization as threats to a transition to a green global economy. Multilateralism, investment in R&D (tech, infrastructure), and traditional financial policies are the cornerstone of the OECD’s green growth agenda.

The OECD states that equality and sustainability must be at the center of economic growth, suggesting that while productivity is still key it is no longer the be all end all of growth. The OECD’s Green Growth Strategy claims that not only that “green” and “growth” can go together, but that they must. The OECD asserts that achieving green growth goals must be the result of coordinated international and institutional cooperation. To this end, the OECD attempts to discredit protectionism and suggests that a multilateral approach must be taken to achieve sustainable development goals. Investment and innovation are central to the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy. They also emphasize the need to better understand the long-term economic cost of inaction in the face of environmental crises and, conversely, the long-term economic benefit of positive action. This is as opposed to simply considering short-term costs and benefits which do not fully reflect the consequences of action or inaction. This analysis includes developing new indicators for growth and strengthening our statistical capacities to interpret such data. Green technology and infrastructure are central to a modern green economy. Once environmental assets and natural resources are valued properly, countries will begin to see that it is in their economic interest to protect the environment.

[SEP] Summary The 1997 World Bank annual report continues to use “development” as the superseding aim of the organization. However, the World bank revised their descriptions for development emphasis in 1997. Instead of using poverty, environment, and economic growth as the areas of emphasis, the Bank broadens their scope to four “networks” for development: Human development; Environmentally and socially sustainable development; finance Private Sector and Infrastructure; Poverty Reduction and Economic Development. The report goes on to describe the Bank’s desire for growth to be something that is environmentally sustainable, as well as socially and economically sustainable. At times in the report, the Bank mentions that “successful economic growth” can lead to environmental issues, and thus does not necessarily draw a positive correlation between economic growth and environmental sustainability. However, the report does suggest that environmentally sustainable economic growth is an underlying aim of World Bank projects and is more likely to be successful growth in the long-term future. Like previous years, the World Bank uses the GEF (Global Environmental Facility) as their main mechanism to start on-the-ground environmental projects and facilitates in the financial management aspects of this grant giving process. In 1997, the Bank’s Economic Development Institute environment program also was active in addressing cross-linking issues of economic growth and environmental sustainability. The report mentions particularly the collaboration with NGOs in seeing progress in environmental initiatives tied to the World Bank’s goals. In many instances the Bank seems to act as a facilitator of conversations between NGOs and other stakeholders over a variety of environmental issues.

[SEP] Summary In 2017, the bank continued to draw links between economic growth, environmental sustainability, and poverty reduction, and emphasized how these three components are integral in creating sustainable development. It highlighted the importance of increasing climate financing. The Bank also stressed how climate change disproportionately affects the most impoverished citizens who are the least economically stable. It views low-carbon development as something that produces a positive feedback loop too: not only does green economic growth contribute to development but this development in turn provides more potential for climate action that generates job creation and economic growth. The 2017 report continued to expand on past environmental and climate initiatives of the past few years. It also began to describe more projects addressing new subsets of environmentally related interests. For example, it addresses the importance of green growth through transportation technology, in the form of increased energy efficiency and low-carbon technological development strategies. It also worked towards greening the financial sector with benchmark bonds and World Bank Green Bonds, which go on to finance environmentally sustainable and renewable energy projects. The Bank continued to increase its carbon emissions transparency and green project transparency by having partners and NGOs assess their work. The Bank also continued with projects that addressed climate related weather risk and damages, in addition to mitigation projects.

They argue that the recovery from the global financial crisis must be undertaken with not only productivity in mind, but also sustainability and equity. For the OECD, economic growth and environmental protection are not opposing forces. Instead, the global economy can foster growth while preserving the environment. The OECD stresses the need to pay equal weight to the economic consequences of environmental policies and the environmental consequences of economic policies. At the heart of the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy is innovation: innovation in green technology and infrastructure. In the wake of the financial crisis, however, public and private investment has plateaued. The OECD calls for a revitalization of investment, both public and private. Increased investment in concert with more traditional measures like subsidy reform, environmental taxes, and emissions trading can lead to significant environmental protection while fostering economic growth. In its role as an international institution, the OECD warns against protectionism and unilateral action. Liberal trade and multilateralism (international and institutional) are at the core of the OECD’s mission and strategy. Goals: “Simply returning to growth will not be sufficient. We must draw all possible lessons from the crisis. We need to do so against a background of climate change, high unemployment levels, particularly among the youth, increasing inequalities, large fiscal deficits and very high debt accumulation. The economic growth model we should champion must take into account the impact on the environment, its redistributive capacity and the international linkages, via trade, investment and migration.” “Indeed, growth remains the key driver for employment and wealth creation. Fair and open markets, competition and innovation are all critical to growth. But we also need a more inclusive and greener model of growth based on sound institutions. Searching for new sources of growth that are also “green”, more equitable and more “gender friendly” has become our common objective to overcome the effects of the crisis.” “These strategic orientations reach beyond the need to find new sources of growth and explore policies to address the employment, social, environmental, and development aspects. The OECD @ 50 is an organisation that strives to improve the prospects of growth and welfare in member and partner countries, that encourages civic participation and equality of opportunities, and that seeks to realign the economy with the environment.” “With about 3% of OECD countries’ potential output lost as a result of the crisis, the time has come for the OECD to develop bold new thinking to address changing economic realities. New sources of balanced, sustainable and equitable growth are necessary. Identifying these new sources of growth and tapping into their full potential is one of our key priorities. Structural reforms will be critical to help enhance the productive capacity of our economies, foster employment, unleash investment and address issues of inclusiveness and social cohesion, so that the benefits of sustained growth are shared equitably.” “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. The OECD’s strategic approach contains much more than growth and recovery – this strategic approach reflects the “stronger”, “cleaner” and “fairer” aspects of our vision and it focuses on our mission of achieving “better policies for better lives” for our citizens.” “The pillars of our substantive focus include macroeconomic policies and financial markets, green growth, innovation, climate change and water, education, employment and skills, social policies, gender equality, migration, governance, anti-corruption and integrity, trade and investment, the OECD Better Life Initiative and a broader OECD development strategy which includes innovation, investment, domestic resource mobilisation, food security, measurement and knowledge sharing.” “Building on the successful results of the COP 16 United Nations Conference on Climate Change in Cancún, we will strengthen our work on climate change, in particular to help countries develop effective and least-cost policy mixes to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In our work on climate change, fossil fuel subsidies and energy-related issues, we will continue to work with the IEA.” “If we can foster a real cross-fertilisation of ideas, it will help us to stay at the frontier of new thinking and ensure we provide relevant and pragmatic advice to governments in their efforts to design and implement better policies for better lives. We also need to continue to produce norms and standards which by their quality and credibility can be embraced by the international community.” Problems: “The world economy is still going through difficult times. The global crisis has left several countries with a legacy of low growth, high unemployment, unsound public finances and lower potential output. Although recovery is underway, it is unbalanced across countries and regions. In most of the emerging economies, high inflation driven by commodity and oil prices is a major concern.” “The food crisis affects all, particularly the poor. Recent natural catastrophes have drawn even more attention to questions about climate change and energy for the future. We are in the midst of a governance upheaval in the MENA [Middle East and North Africa] region, the full implications of which are still unknown. We do know, however, that poverty, income gaps, high unemployment, food insecurity, lack of education and gender inequality all matter for governance outcomes. These challenges call for strong and collective action. The OECD will contribute with well-developed forms of co-operation and engagement.” “Advanced, emerging and developing countries will face different challenges and opportunities, as will countries with differing economic and political circumstances. There are, on the other hand, common considerations that need to be addressed in all settings. Making green growth work, implementing the strategy and supporting member and partner countries in their policies for a greener growth path will figure among OECD’s top strategic priorities for the next few years.” “Poverty prevents most of the world’s hungry population from accessing food. This becomes a vicious circle, as food insecurity then threatens social cohesion and political stability; and not just in the region most immediately affected by supply shortfalls. The recent hikes in food prices have only aggravated this longstanding problem.” “We need to continue to show that there is added value in multilateral co-operation rather than acting unilaterally. We also need to strengthen our co-operation with other international organisations. We proposed the creation of a network for co-operation on policy coherence, bringing together the international organisations involved in the G20 (IMF, World Bank, FSB, ILO, WTO and OECD). The objective would be to improve co-ordination and exchange of information among international organisations.” “One key challenge in the past year has been finding a way to make the case for green growth. Governments have made it clear that unless they can deliver economic growth at the same time as meeting environmental challenges, they stand little chance of implementing ambitious new policies. We need to be equally concerned about the environmental impact of economic policies and the economic impact of environmental policies. The Green Growth project will operationalise that for the first time.” Policies: “The OECD Green Growth Strategy, to be launched at this year’s Ministerial, aims to develop an actionable policy framework with specific tools and recommendations in a broad range of areas, including fiscal, innovation, trade, labour and social policies to help governments achieve the most efficient shift to greener growth. Innovation will play a key role in this shift. Greening the growth path of an economy depends on policy and institutional settings, level of development, resource endowments and particular environmental pressure points.” “Our pioneering work on a comprehensive policy mix, including the use of economic instruments such as taxes and emission trading schemes, provides the main tools needed in the fight against climate change. There is already evidence of leading companies shifting to a low-carbon business model, starting with measuring their greenhouse gas emissions and then taking action to reduce them, and the OECD will continue to examine the policies and conditions that can best incentivise private sector action.” “Considering the recent accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, we should work through the NEA on strengthening safety standards for both existing and future plants and ensuring that all the lessons from this accident are incorporated. This would help alleviate public concerns and allow nuclear power to continue to play an important role in the global energy mix and in the fight against climate change.” “We will build on the OECD’s role as the premier forum for monitoring international public finance flows, to develop systems for better tracking private financing and to assess the options for scaling-up financing for climate change. We will also continue our strong commitment to providing policy guidance on improving water policy through our work on the economic, institutional and policy responses to the water challenge.” “Improving agricultural productivity and the functioning of local and global agricultural markets as well as the liberalisation of trade are essential. But durable solutions will also feature improvements in systems of governance and the overall business environment in developing countries and increased investments in health, education and physical infrastructure.” “We will continue to support the G20 on the following priorities: on the adoption of structural policies within the Framework for Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth; on policies for employment, skills and jobs; on policies to liberalise trade, investment and capital flows; on the promotion and adoption of standards for anti-corruption; on the abolishment of fossil fuel subsidies; on policies for efficient, fair and transparent taxation systems; on food security and commodity markets; and on the Seoul Consensus for Shared Growth and its Multi-Year-Action Plan.” “There is a good reason why ‘innovation’ is one of today’s most common buzzwords in public policy. It is an important method for fuelling economic growth and addressing urgent social challenges like climate change and ageing societies. Stimulating innovation is not about spending money – it is about better co-ordination, long-term policy commitment, breaking down barriers and meeting people’s needs. Through its work on innovation, science, technology and industry, the OECD strives to deliver the most effective policy recommendations on key emerging issues facing governments.” “Rising commodity prices are again having a devastating impact on low income households around the world; immediate humanitarian relief is needed. But governments must also act to address the fundamental cause of global food insecurity: poverty. This means improving systems of governance and the overall business environment in less developed economies, to encourage widespread growth and employment; increasing public and private investment in developing country agriculture, in particular to increase productivity; and opening agricultural markets so that products can flow from surplus to deficit areas.”

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2012 Summary: The 2012 OECD Annual Report stresses the fact that economic growth and environmental sustainability do not constitute a “zero sum game.” That is to say, an improvement in one does not necessarily detract from the other. In fact, the OECD claims that the two go hand-in-hand. In light of the global financial crisis, the OECD recognizes the need to rebuild national economies and restore global growth. In doing so, however, productivity cannot be the only metric we take into account as far as growth is concerned--we must also consider equity and sustainability. Technological innovation, which is achieved through investment, is key to the greening of the global economy. To foster a productive, sustainable, and equitable global economy, the OECD points to the development of their Green Growth Strategy and Rio+20 as examples of efficacious international cooperation. Multilateralism is the way of the future for the OECD. Accordingly, they argue that protectionism and beggar-thy-neighbor policies are impediments to creating sustainable development. Liberal multilateral trade must underpin any effort to green the global economy. Education, skills training, and knowledge sharing are all identified as critical undertakings for the OECD. Efforts will also be bolstered by the proper valuation of environmental assets.
