In the wake of the financial crisis, however, public and private investment has plateaued. The OECD calls for a revitalization of investment, both public and private. Increased investment in concert with more traditional measures like subsidy reform, environmental taxes, and emissions trading can lead to significant environmental protection while fostering economic growth. In its role as an international institution, the OECD warns against protectionism and unilateral action. Liberal trade and multilateralism (international and institutional) are at the core of the OECD’s mission and strategy. Goals: “Simply returning to growth will not be sufficient. We must draw all possible lessons from the crisis. We need to do so against a background of climate change, high unemployment levels, particularly among the youth, increasing inequalities, large fiscal deficits and very high debt accumulation. The economic growth model we should champion must take into account the impact on the environment, its redistributive capacity and the international linkages, via trade, investment and migration.” “Indeed, growth remains the key driver for employment and wealth creation. Fair and open markets, competition and innovation are all critical to growth. But we also need a more inclusive and greener model of growth based on sound institutions. Searching for new sources of growth that are also “green”, more equitable and more “gender friendly” has become our common objective to overcome the effects of the crisis.” “These strategic orientations reach beyond the need to find new sources of growth and explore policies to address the employment, social, environmental, and development aspects. The OECD @ 50 is an organisation that strives to improve the prospects of growth and welfare in member and partner countries, that encourages civic participation and equality of opportunities, and that seeks to realign the economy with the environment.” “With about 3% of OECD countries’ potential output lost as a result of the crisis, the time has come for the OECD to develop bold new thinking to address changing economic realities. New sources of balanced, sustainable and equitable growth are necessary. Identifying these new sources of growth and tapping into their full potential is one of our key priorities. Structural reforms will be critical to help enhance the productive capacity of our economies, foster employment, unleash investment and address issues of inclusiveness and social cohesion, so that the benefits of sustained growth are shared equitably.” “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. The OECD’s strategic approach contains much more than growth and recovery – this strategic approach reflects the “stronger”, “cleaner” and “fairer” aspects of our vision and it focuses on our mission of achieving “better policies for better lives” for our citizens.” “The pillars of our substantive focus include macroeconomic policies and financial markets, green growth, innovation, climate change and water, education, employment and skills, social policies, gender equality, migration, governance, anti-corruption and integrity, trade and investment, the OECD Better Life Initiative and a broader OECD development strategy which includes innovation, investment, domestic resource mobilisation, food security, measurement and knowledge sharing.” “Building on the successful results of the COP 16 United Nations Conference on Climate Change in Cancún, we will strengthen our work on climate change, in particular to help countries develop effective and least-cost policy mixes to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In our work on climate change, fossil fuel subsidies and energy-related issues, we will continue to work with the IEA.” “If we can foster a real cross-fertilisation of ideas, it will help us to stay at the frontier of new thinking and ensure we provide relevant and pragmatic advice to governments in their efforts to design and implement better policies for better lives. We also need to continue to produce norms and standards which by their quality and credibility can be embraced by the international community.” Problems: “The world economy is still going through difficult times. The global crisis has left several countries with a legacy of low growth, high unemployment, unsound public finances and lower potential output. Although recovery is underway, it is unbalanced across countries and regions. In most of the emerging economies, high inflation driven by commodity and oil prices is a major concern.” “The food crisis affects all, particularly the poor. Recent natural catastrophes have drawn even more attention to questions about climate change and energy for the future. We are in the midst of a governance upheaval in the MENA [Middle East and North Africa] region, the full implications of which are still unknown. We do know, however, that poverty, income gaps, high unemployment, food insecurity, lack of education and gender inequality all matter for governance outcomes. These challenges call for strong and collective action. The OECD will contribute with well-developed forms of co-operation and engagement.” “Advanced, emerging and developing countries will face different challenges and opportunities, as will countries with differing economic and political circumstances. There are, on the other hand, common considerations that need to be addressed in all settings. Making green growth work, implementing the strategy and supporting member and partner countries in their policies for a greener growth path will figure among OECD’s top strategic priorities for the next few years.” “Poverty prevents most of the world’s hungry population from accessing food. This becomes a vicious circle, as food insecurity then threatens social cohesion and political stability; and not just in the region most immediately affected by supply shortfalls. The recent hikes in food prices have only aggravated this longstanding problem.” “We need to continue to show that there is added value in multilateral co-operation rather than acting unilaterally. We also need to strengthen our co-operation with other international organisations. We proposed the creation of a network for co-operation on policy coherence, bringing together the international organisations involved in the G20 (IMF, World Bank, FSB, ILO, WTO and OECD). The objective would be to improve co-ordination and exchange of information among international organisations.” “One key challenge in the past year has been finding a way to make the case for green growth. Governments have made it clear that unless they can deliver economic growth at the same time as meeting environmental challenges, they stand little chance of implementing ambitious new policies. We need to be equally concerned about the environmental impact of economic policies and the economic impact of environmental policies. The Green Growth project will operationalise that for the first time.” Policies: “The OECD Green Growth Strategy, to be launched at this year’s Ministerial, aims to develop an actionable policy framework with specific tools and recommendations in a broad range of areas, including fiscal, innovation, trade, labour and social policies to help governments achieve the most efficient shift to greener growth. Innovation will play a key role in this shift. Greening the growth path of an economy depends on policy and institutional settings, level of development, resource endowments and particular environmental pressure points.” “Our pioneering work on a comprehensive policy mix, including the use of economic instruments such as taxes and emission trading schemes, provides the main tools needed in the fight against climate change. There is already evidence of leading companies shifting to a low-carbon business model, starting with measuring their greenhouse gas emissions and then taking action to reduce them, and the OECD will continue to examine the policies and conditions that can best incentivise private sector action.” “Considering the recent accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, we should work through the NEA on strengthening safety standards for both existing and future plants and ensuring that all the lessons from this accident are incorporated. This would help alleviate public concerns and allow nuclear power to continue to play an important role in the global energy mix and in the fight against climate change.” “We will build on the OECD’s role as the premier forum for monitoring international public finance flows, to develop systems for better tracking private financing and to assess the options for scaling-up financing for climate change. We will also continue our strong commitment to providing policy guidance on improving water policy through our work on the economic, institutional and policy responses to the water challenge.” “Improving agricultural productivity and the functioning of local and global agricultural markets as well as the liberalisation of trade are essential. But durable solutions will also feature improvements in systems of governance and the overall business environment in developing countries and increased investments in health, education and physical infrastructure.” “We will continue to support the G20 on the following priorities: on the adoption of structural policies within the Framework for Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth; on policies for employment, skills and jobs; on policies to liberalise trade, investment and capital flows; on the promotion and adoption of standards for anti-corruption; on the abolishment of fossil fuel subsidies; on policies for efficient, fair and transparent taxation systems; on food security and commodity markets; and on the Seoul Consensus for Shared Growth and its Multi-Year-Action Plan.” “There is a good reason why ‘innovation’ is one of today’s most common buzzwords in public policy. It is an important method for fuelling economic growth and addressing urgent social challenges like climate change and ageing societies. Stimulating innovation is not about spending money – it is about better co-ordination, long-term policy commitment, breaking down barriers and meeting people’s needs. Through its work on innovation, science, technology and industry, the OECD strives to deliver the most effective policy recommendations on key emerging issues facing governments.” “Rising commodity prices are again having a devastating impact on low income households around the world; immediate humanitarian relief is needed. But governments must also act to address the fundamental cause of global food insecurity: poverty. This means improving systems of governance and the overall business environment in less developed economies, to encourage widespread growth and employment; increasing public and private investment in developing country agriculture, in particular to increase productivity; and opening agricultural markets so that products can flow from surplus to deficit areas.”

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2015 Summary: The OECD’s 2015 Annual Report highlights the work of the OECD in the move towards sustainable development, through what they call green growth policies. They assert that there is no tradeoff between environmental protection and economic growth--in fact, they suggest that the two go hand-in-hand. The Strategic Orientations of the Secretary-General lay out the OECD’s desire for a transition to a low-carbon global economy which, in their words, will offer sustainability and resilience in the face of crisis like climate change. A section of the report is dedicated to the Ministerial Council Statement regarding Climate Change. Here, the council reaffirms the need for coordinated international cooperation (e.g. OECD, IEA, NEA, ITF, UNFCCC) in the transition to a low-carbon economy. Through international institutional alignment and cooperation, the OECD believes that national governments will have clear indicators as to the future trajectory of global economy. The Ministerial Council statement lays out a variety of policy proposals to achieve their goal. These include investment in technological R&D, investment in infrastructure, subsidy reform, and strengthening international trade to name a few. In the Key Activities section of the Report, the OECD mentions their continued development of the Green Growth Strategy, which is a staple of their Annual Reports. Here, the OECD again makes clear that governments can foster economic growth while protecting national environments. Per usual, the report also includes sections pertaining to the work of the Environment and the Trade and Agriculture Directorates. The Environment Directorate reiterates the OECD’s work in promoting investment in green technology and infrastructure. The Trade and Agriculture Directorate mentions agriculture (e.g. fisheries) as a sector of the economy which is especially conducive to the simultaneous improvements in sustainability and productivity. Multilateral trade can help ensure that suppliers meet demand while maintaining sustainable resource use. Goals: “Countries are taking steps towards green growth; yet much more determined efforts are needed to integrate environmental priorities into economic agendas to promote sustainable growth and well- being. The OECD report Towards Green Growth? Tracking Progress aims to accelerate countries’ implementation of green growth policies by providing more targeted and coherent policy advice.” (13-14) “The guidance emerging from country experience, the enriched Green Growth Strategy and lessons learnt from the OECD mainstreaming process are intended to serve as tools to this end. Going forward, the report will help target policy advice by highlighting priority areas for further analysis and opportunities to enhance mainstreaming at the OECD and beyond.” “Reinforcing our existing efforts and using the OECD’s research and evidence-based analysis, including under the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy, to help us to pursue ambitious and cost- effective policies with a view to doing our part to limit effectively the increase in global temperature below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and simultaneously supporting the recovery from the economic and financial crisis” (38-39) “Ahead of COP20 and COP21, we invite the OECD, in co-operation with the International Energy Agency (IEA), the Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) and the International Transport Forum (ITF), to continue to support the UNFCCC negotiations and to examine how to better align policies across different areas for a successful economic transition of all countries to sustainable low-carbon and climate-resilient economies and report to the 2015 OECD Ministerial Council Meeting.” “The Environment Directorate helps countries design and implement effective policies to address environmental problems and sustainably manage natural resources. It examines the linkages between the environment and economic, sectoral or social concerns in areas such as climate change; biodiversity; water; waste; environmental taxes; safety of chemicals, nanomaterials and genetically modi ed crops; agriculture; transport; trade; investment; and development.” “The forthcoming OECD-IEA-ITF-NEA report Aligning Policies for a Low-Carbon Economy provides guidance for governments to align incentives across policy areas to help catalyse reform. As shown by OECD work on Environmental Policies and Productivity Growth, economic growth does not need to be traded for environmental stringency.”

[SEP] OECD Annual Report 2009 Summary: The 2009 OECD Annual Report highlights the need to develop a “cleaner” global economy in the wake of the financial crisis. “Cleaner” has two meanings for the OECD: first, anti-corruption efforts and strengthening corporate governance to create a cleaner globalization and second, fighting environmental degradation and climate change to create a cleaner world. The OECD presents efforts to reduce greenhouse gases as “economically rational”, demonstrating a strong linkage between sustainability and economic development. They further stress that delays in action now will only result in higher costs in the future. The OECD cites investment in eco-innovation as a “win-win” scenario as it leads to the development of environmentally friendly technology while simultaneously acting as a source of growth. To this end, they propose incentivizing R&D in green technology. The report also emphasizes the need to maintain open markets and international trade, arguing that liberalization is the best way to achieve growth and security. The OECD recognizes the need to develop better market tools to help in the pricing of environmental externalities (e.g. carbon tax) as well as restimulating public investment in green R&D. They also propose cap-and-trade as a policy which can identify the cheapest possible abatement opportunities. Goals: “This crisis presents opportunities as well as challenges, and the OECD is seizing these opportunities to formulate policies that will lead to a stronger, cleaner, fairer world economy. over the past year, the OECD has pressed for a “stronger” world economy through its work in areas such as regulation; governance; trade (especially Doha); investment and competition; and, of course, developing policies for sustainable growth. Work on anti-corruption, corporate governance and tax evasion has sought to restore trust in globalisation by making it “cleaner”. so has, literally, our work on environment and climate change, another face of “cleaner”. “Ministers suggested, variously, that future work could analyse and compare concrete national and international policy options to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions from a wide range of activities; analyse incentives for major emitters to take part in international action, including understanding the impacts of climate change on different regions and sectors, and the benefits and co-benefits of action; assess the impact of alternative policies on competitiveness, carbon leakage, financing, technological development and transfer; consider how policies could provide certainty to private investors and remain flexible at the same time; and analyse the economic costs, benefits and distributive aspects of climate change adaptation and mitigation policies.” “OECD work confirms that tackling climate change should not be delayed, and that ambitious action to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is economically rational. The economic crisis provides no room for complacency. at most, it might slightly reduce global emissions temporarily, after which an upward trend will resume. delaying action on climate change would only mean larger cuts later.” “Concerns about the potential carbon leakage and competitiveness impacts of climate policies are often exaggerated. unless only very few countries take action against climate change, carbon leakage rates and competitiveness effects of climate policies are very small … Border tax adjustments or grandfathering domestic emission permits can reduce carbon leakage, but at a cost overall to the economy. If carefully designed, sector-wide agreements covering energy- intensive industries may offer a cheaper and more constructive alternative to mitigate fears of leakage.” “The economic downturn should not weaken efforts to achieve the long-term goal of a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy. The crisis instead presents an opportunity to move towards a stronger, cleaner and fairer world economy. It provides incentives to improve efficiency in the use of energy and materials by getting the prices right, and an opportunity to remove environmentally harmful subsidies, for example, to fossil fuel production and consumption, benefiting both the environment and public budgets.” “Investment in eco-friendly technologies can represent a new source of growth and “win-win” opportunities for both the environment and economic recovery. New low-carbon technologies are key to reducing the future costs of climate change mitigation. stimulus packages could support eco-innovation. examples include offering fiscal incentives for R&D in green technologies.”

[SEP] Summary The UNEP’s 2001 Annual Report focuses on the proper ways to handle globalization at the turn of the century. Specifically how to do so in a manner that decreases the poverty and fear affecting billions of people across the world, and ensure that globalisation benefits them all. It stresses that the question of how best to manage the environment is integral to our future development, and that the Earth’s limited resources and fragile ecosystems must be respected for a sustainable future. The UNEP proposes that if we maintain a viable global environment, and build healthy, equitable societies, that Governments, United Nations entities, the private sector and civil society will have to work together to achieve sustainable development. To combat the issue of poverty and attempting to reduce it, the UNEP argues that we must first focus on addressing the issue of consumption. As such, a central goal of the organization is alleviating poverty in a way that doesn't encourage a massive increase in unsustainable consumption. Similarly, how to reduce the excessive consumption of the minority without harming lifestyles that depend on that consumption. Through the new working groups on Climate Change and the Agenda 21 initiatives, the UNEP is attempting to encourage increased civil society engagement, complemented with a greater commitment from the private sector, to improve environmental performance in a way that harnesses both human and natural capital. In this report, the UNEP affirms its commitment to guiding the world towards a sustainable future by providing easily accessible environmental information based on the newest technologies, developing policy instruments and coordinating multilateral environmental agreements. It also pledges to work with governments and the private sector to promote best public/private practices and clean technology transfer to ensure equitable development and economic progress among all nations in an environmentally beneficial way.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2011 Summary: The environment plays a major role in the OECD’s 2011 Annual Report. They argue that the recovery from the global financial crisis must be undertaken with not only productivity in mind, but also sustainability and equity. For the OECD, economic growth and environmental protection are not opposing forces. Instead, the global economy can foster growth while preserving the environment. The OECD stresses the need to pay equal weight to the economic consequences of environmental policies and the environmental consequences of economic policies. At the heart of the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy is innovation: innovation in green technology and infrastructure. In the wake of the financial crisis, however, public and private investment has plateaued. The OECD calls for a revitalization of investment, both public and private. Increased investment in concert with more traditional measures like subsidy reform, environmental taxes, and emissions trading can lead to significant environmental protection while fostering economic growth. In its role as an international institution, the OECD warns against protectionism and unilateral action. Liberal trade and multilateralism (international and institutional) are at the core of the OECD’s mission and strategy. Goals: “Simply returning to growth will not be sufficient. We must draw all possible lessons from the crisis. We need to do so against a background of climate change, high unemployment levels, particularly among the youth, increasing inequalities, large fiscal deficits and very high debt accumulation. The economic growth model we should champion must take into account the impact on the environment, its redistributive capacity and the international linkages, via trade, investment and migration.” “Indeed, growth remains the key driver for employment and wealth creation. Fair and open markets, competition and innovation are all critical to growth. But we also need a more inclusive and greener model of growth based on sound institutions. Searching for new sources of growth that are also “green”, more equitable and more “gender friendly” has become our common objective to overcome the effects of the crisis.” “These strategic orientations reach beyond the need to find new sources of growth and explore policies to address the employment, social, environmental, and development aspects. The OECD @ 50 is an organisation that strives to improve the prospects of growth and welfare in member and partner countries, that encourages civic participation and equality of opportunities, and that seeks to realign the economy with the environment.” “With about 3% of OECD countries’ potential output lost as a result of the crisis, the time has come for the OECD to develop bold new thinking to address changing economic realities. New sources of balanced, sustainable and equitable growth are necessary. Identifying these new sources of growth and tapping into their full potential is one of our key priorities. Structural reforms will be critical to help enhance the productive capacity of our economies, foster employment, unleash investment and address issues of inclusiveness and social cohesion, so that the benefits of sustained growth are shared equitably.” “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. The OECD’s strategic approach contains much more than growth and recovery – this strategic approach reflects the “stronger”, “cleaner” and “fairer” aspects of our vision and it focuses on our mission of achieving “better policies for better lives” for our citizens.” “The pillars of our substantive focus include macroeconomic policies and financial markets, green growth, innovation, climate change and water, education, employment and skills, social policies, gender equality, migration, governance, anti-corruption and integrity, trade and investment, the OECD Better Life Initiative and a broader OECD development strategy which includes innovation, investment, domestic resource mobilisation, food security, measurement and knowledge sharing.” “Building on the successful results of the COP 16 United Nations Conference on Climate Change in Cancún, we will strengthen our work on climate change, in particular to help countries develop effective and least-cost policy mixes to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In our work on climate change, fossil fuel subsidies and energy-related issues, we will continue to work with the IEA.” “If we can foster a real cross-fertilisation of ideas, it will help us to stay at the frontier of new thinking and ensure we provide relevant and pragmatic advice to governments in their efforts to design and implement better policies for better lives. We also need to continue to produce norms and standards which by their quality and credibility can be embraced by the international community.” Problems: “The world economy is still going through difficult times. The global crisis has left several countries with a legacy of low growth, high unemployment, unsound public finances and lower potential output. Although recovery is underway, it is unbalanced across countries and regions. In most of the emerging economies, high inflation driven by commodity and oil prices is a major concern.” “The food crisis affects all, particularly the poor. Recent natural catastrophes have drawn even more attention to questions about climate change and energy for the future. We are in the midst of a governance upheaval in the MENA [Middle East and North Africa] region, the full implications of which are still unknown. We do know, however, that poverty, income gaps, high unemployment, food insecurity, lack of education and gender inequality all matter for governance outcomes. These challenges call for strong and collective action. The OECD will contribute with well-developed forms of co-operation and engagement.” “Advanced, emerging and developing countries will face different challenges and opportunities, as will countries with differing economic and political circumstances. There are, on the other hand, common considerations that need to be addressed in all settings. Making green growth work, implementing the strategy and supporting member and partner countries in their policies for a greener growth path will figure among OECD’s top strategic priorities for the next few years.” “Poverty prevents most of the world’s hungry population from accessing food. This becomes a vicious circle, as food insecurity then threatens social cohesion and political stability; and not just in the region most immediately affected by supply shortfalls. The recent hikes in food prices have only aggravated this longstanding problem.” “We need to continue to show that there is added value in multilateral co-operation rather than acting unilaterally. We also need to strengthen our co-operation with other international organisations. We proposed the creation of a network for co-operation on policy coherence, bringing together the international organisations involved in the G20 (IMF, World Bank, FSB, ILO, WTO and OECD). The objective would be to improve co-ordination and exchange of information among international organisations.” “One key challenge in the past year has been finding a way to make the case for green growth. Governments have made it clear that unless they can deliver economic growth at the same time as meeting environmental challenges, they stand little chance of implementing ambitious new policies. We need to be equally concerned about the environmental impact of economic policies and the economic impact of environmental policies. The Green Growth project will operationalise that for the first time.” Policies: “The OECD Green Growth Strategy, to be launched at this year’s Ministerial, aims to develop an actionable policy framework with specific tools and recommendations in a broad range of areas, including fiscal, innovation, trade, labour and social policies to help governments achieve the most efficient shift to greener growth. [SEP] UNDP Annual Report 2002 Summary: The 2002 UNDP Annual Report highlights the inclusion of environmental sustainability in the organization’s Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). The UNDP directly ties sustainable development to their notion of economic recovery. The report stresses the need for local governments to take action and promotes a decentralized vision of achieving sustainable development at the community level. To this end, the UNDP encourages the development of public-private partnerships as well as the engagement of civil society organizations to produce innovative policies. They also point to volunteerism as a key aspect of achieving the MDGs. The report recognizes the challenges posed by the lack of financial and political support and calls for a remobilization of these assets. Furthermore, the UNDP sees international coordination as the only way to sufficiently address truly global environmental problems (e.g. climate change, biodiversity loss, ozone depletion). They also recognize that the poor are the most adversely affected by environmental degradation, thus rendering the need for international cooperation even more urgent. The UNDP points to its development of sustainable energy policy as well as its help in the implementation of the Montreal Protocol as examples of its initiatives. Lastly, they stress the need to build the technological and informational infrastructure necessary for communities to map out plans for sustainable development. Goals: “The results [of UNDP Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)] are visible where they matter most: in our increased capacity to provide cutting-edge development services and programmes monitored and measured by a pioneering results-based management system; in our growing global leadership in generating the demand for better public policy on issues from democratic governance to sustainable energy; and, ultimately, in the greater extent to which we are helping countries build their own capacity to manage development issues.” “Ensure environmental sustainability: More than one billion people still lack access to safe drinking water— but nearly one billion gained access to safe water, and one billion gained access to sanitation, during the 1990s.” “True recovery includes: sustainable development, restoration of essential services, implementation by local governments and CSOs [Civil Society Organization], decentralized planning, risk management and reduction.” “UNDP helps countries strengthen their capacity to address these [environmental] challenges at global, national and community levels, seeking out and sharing best practices, providing innovative policy advice and linking partners through pilot projects that help poor people build sustainable livelihoods.” “Administered by UNDP, the United Nations Volunteers (UNV) programme promotes volunteer action around the world, demonstrating the role volunteerism can play in development.” “NGOs such as the Regional Environment Centre in Hungary are strengthening public involvement in environment-related decision-making and raising awareness in local communities. Every member of the strategic partnership has comparative advantages and a role to play; through UNDP leadership, each can learn from the other, and all are more effective.”

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2015 Summary: The OECD’s 2015 Annual Report highlights the work of the OECD in the move towards sustainable development, through what they call green growth policies. They assert that there is no tradeoff between environmental protection and economic growth--in fact, they suggest that the two go hand-in-hand. The Strategic Orientations of the Secretary-General lay out the OECD’s desire for a transition to a low-carbon global economy which, in their words, will offer sustainability and resilience in the face of crisis like climate change. A section of the report is dedicated to the Ministerial Council Statement regarding Climate Change. Here, the council reaffirms the need for coordinated international cooperation (e.g. OECD, IEA, NEA, ITF, UNFCCC) in the transition to a low-carbon economy. Through international institutional alignment and cooperation, the OECD believes that national governments will have clear indicators as to the future trajectory of global economy. The Ministerial Council statement lays out a variety of policy proposals to achieve their goal. These include investment in technological R&D, investment in infrastructure, subsidy reform, and strengthening international trade to name a few. In the Key Activities section of the Report, the OECD mentions their continued development of the Green Growth Strategy, which is a staple of their Annual Reports. Here, the OECD again makes clear that governments can foster economic growth while protecting national environments. Per usual, the report also includes sections pertaining to the work of the Environment and the Trade and Agriculture Directorates. The Environment Directorate reiterates the OECD’s work in promoting investment in green technology and infrastructure. The Trade and Agriculture Directorate mentions agriculture (e.g. fisheries) as a sector of the economy which is especially conducive to the simultaneous improvements in sustainability and productivity. Multilateral trade can help ensure that suppliers meet demand while maintaining sustainable resource use. Goals: “Countries are taking steps towards green growth; yet much more determined efforts are needed to integrate environmental priorities into economic agendas to promote sustainable growth and well- being. The OECD report Towards Green Growth? Tracking Progress aims to accelerate countries’ implementation of green growth policies by providing more targeted and coherent policy advice.” (13-14) “The guidance emerging from country experience, the enriched Green Growth Strategy and lessons learnt from the OECD mainstreaming process are intended to serve as tools to this end. [SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2011 Summary: The environment plays a major role in the OECD’s 2011 Annual Report. They argue that the recovery from the global financial crisis must be undertaken with not only productivity in mind, but also sustainability and equity. For the OECD, economic growth and environmental protection are not opposing forces. Instead, the global economy can foster growth while preserving the environment. The OECD stresses the need to pay equal weight to the economic consequences of environmental policies and the environmental consequences of economic policies. At the heart of the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy is innovation: innovation in green technology and infrastructure. In the wake of the financial crisis, however, public and private investment has plateaued. The OECD calls for a revitalization of investment, both public and private. Increased investment in concert with more traditional measures like subsidy reform, environmental taxes, and emissions trading can lead to significant environmental protection while fostering economic growth. In its role as an international institution, the OECD warns against protectionism and unilateral action. Liberal trade and multilateralism (international and institutional) are at the core of the OECD’s mission and strategy. Goals: “Simply returning to growth will not be sufficient. We must draw all possible lessons from the crisis. We need to do so against a background of climate change, high unemployment levels, particularly among the youth, increasing inequalities, large fiscal deficits and very high debt accumulation. The economic growth model we should champion must take into account the impact on the environment, its redistributive capacity and the international linkages, via trade, investment and migration.” “Indeed, growth remains the key driver for employment and wealth creation. Fair and open markets, competition and innovation are all critical to growth. But we also need a more inclusive and greener model of growth based on sound institutions. Searching for new sources of growth that are also “green”, more equitable and more “gender friendly” has become our common objective to overcome the effects of the crisis.” “These strategic orientations reach beyond the need to find new sources of growth and explore policies to address the employment, social, environmental, and development aspects. The OECD @ 50 is an organisation that strives to improve the prospects of growth and welfare in member and partner countries, that encourages civic participation and equality of opportunities, and that seeks to realign the economy with the environment.” “With about 3% of OECD countries’ potential output lost as a result of the crisis, the time has come for the OECD to develop bold new thinking to address changing economic realities. New sources of balanced, sustainable and equitable growth are necessary. Identifying these new sources of growth and tapping into their full potential is one of our key priorities. Structural reforms will be critical to help enhance the productive capacity of our economies, foster employment, unleash investment and address issues of inclusiveness and social cohesion, so that the benefits of sustained growth are shared equitably.” “Inclusive and green growth should permeate our thinking. The OECD’s strategic approach contains much more than growth and recovery – this strategic approach reflects the “stronger”, “cleaner” and “fairer” aspects of our vision and it focuses on our mission of achieving “better policies for better lives” for our citizens.” “The pillars of our substantive focus include macroeconomic policies and financial markets, green growth, innovation, climate change and water, education, employment and skills, social policies, gender equality, migration, governance, anti-corruption and integrity, trade and investment, the OECD Better Life Initiative and a broader OECD development strategy which includes innovation, investment, domestic resource mobilisation, food security, measurement and knowledge sharing.” “Building on the successful results of the COP 16 United Nations Conference on Climate Change in Cancún, we will strengthen our work on climate change, in particular to help countries develop effective and least-cost policy mixes to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In our work on climate change, fossil fuel subsidies and energy-related issues, we will continue to work with the IEA.” “If we can foster a real cross-fertilisation of ideas, it will help us to stay at the frontier of new thinking and ensure we provide relevant and pragmatic advice to governments in their efforts to design and implement better policies for better lives. We also need to continue to produce norms and standards which by their quality and credibility can be embraced by the international community.” Problems: “The world economy is still going through difficult times. The global crisis has left several countries with a legacy of low growth, high unemployment, unsound public finances and lower potential output. Although recovery is underway, it is unbalanced across countries and regions. In most of the emerging economies, high inflation driven by commodity and oil prices is a major concern.” “The food crisis affects all, particularly the poor. Recent natural catastrophes have drawn even more attention to questions about climate change and energy for the future. We are in the midst of a governance upheaval in the MENA [Middle East and North Africa] region, the full implications of which are still unknown. We do know, however, that poverty, income gaps, high unemployment, food insecurity, lack of education and gender inequality all matter for governance outcomes. These challenges call for strong and collective action. The OECD will contribute with well-developed forms of co-operation and engagement.” “Advanced, emerging and developing countries will face different challenges and opportunities, as will countries with differing economic and political circumstances. There are, on the other hand, common considerations that need to be addressed in all settings. Making green growth work, implementing the strategy and supporting member and partner countries in their policies for a greener growth path will figure among OECD’s top strategic priorities for the next few years.” “Poverty prevents most of the world’s hungry population from accessing food. This becomes a vicious circle, as food insecurity then threatens social cohesion and political stability; and not just in the region most immediately affected by supply shortfalls. The recent hikes in food prices have only aggravated this longstanding problem.” “We need to continue to show that there is added value in multilateral co-operation rather than acting unilaterally. We also need to strengthen our co-operation with other international organisations. We proposed the creation of a network for co-operation on policy coherence, bringing together the international organisations involved in the G20 (IMF, World Bank, FSB, ILO, WTO and OECD). The objective would be to improve co-ordination and exchange of information among international organisations.” “One key challenge in the past year has been finding a way to make the case for green growth. Governments have made it clear that unless they can deliver economic growth at the same time as meeting environmental challenges, they stand little chance of implementing ambitious new policies. We need to be equally concerned about the environmental impact of economic policies and the economic impact of environmental policies. The Green Growth project will operationalise that for the first time.” Policies: “The OECD Green Growth Strategy, to be launched at this year’s Ministerial, aims to develop an actionable policy framework with specific tools and recommendations in a broad range of areas, including fiscal, innovation, trade, labour and social policies to help governments achieve the most efficient shift to greener growth. Innovation will play a key role in this shift. Greening the growth path of an economy depends on policy and institutional settings, level of development, resource endowments and particular environmental pressure points.” “Our pioneering work on a comprehensive policy mix, including the use of economic instruments such as taxes and emission trading schemes, provides the main tools needed in the fight against climate change. There is already evidence of leading companies shifting to a low-carbon business model, starting with measuring their greenhouse gas emissions and then taking action to reduce them, and the OECD will continue to examine the policies and conditions that can best incentivise private sector action.” “Considering the recent accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, we should work through the NEA on strengthening safety standards for both existing and future plants and ensuring that all the lessons from this accident are incorporated. This would help alleviate public concerns and allow nuclear power to continue to play an important role in the global energy mix and in the fight against climate change.” “We will build on the OECD’s role as the premier forum for monitoring international public finance flows, to develop systems for better tracking private financing and to assess the options for scaling-up financing for climate change. We will also continue our strong commitment to providing policy guidance on improving water policy through our work on the economic, institutional and policy responses to the water challenge.” “Improving agricultural productivity and the functioning of local and global agricultural markets as well as the liberalisation of trade are essential. But durable solutions will also feature improvements in systems of governance and the overall business environment in developing countries and increased investments in health, education and physical infrastructure.” “We will continue to support the G20 on the following priorities: on the adoption of structural policies within the Framework for Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth; on policies for employment, skills and jobs; on policies to liberalise trade, investment and capital flows; on the promotion and adoption of standards for anti-corruption; on the abolishment of fossil fuel subsidies; on policies for efficient, fair and transparent taxation systems; on food security and commodity markets; and on the Seoul Consensus for Shared Growth and its Multi-Year-Action Plan.” “There is a good reason why ‘innovation’ is one of today’s most common buzzwords in public policy. It is an important method for fuelling economic growth and addressing urgent social challenges like climate change and ageing societies. Stimulating innovation is not about spending money – it is about better co-ordination, long-term policy commitment, breaking down barriers and meeting people’s needs. Through its work on innovation, science, technology and industry, the OECD strives to deliver the most effective policy recommendations on key emerging issues facing governments.” “Rising commodity prices are again having a devastating impact on low income households around the world; immediate humanitarian relief is needed. But governments must also act to address the fundamental cause of global food insecurity: poverty. This means improving systems of governance and the overall business environment in less developed economies, to encourage widespread growth and employment; increasing public and private investment in developing country agriculture, in particular to increase productivity; and opening agricultural markets so that products can flow from surplus to deficit areas.”

[SEP] Summary Like previous years, the 2006 annual report continues to view poverty reduction, economic growth, and environmental sustainability as objective aims that must be sought in tandem to one another. It describes the ongoing dilemma that climate change is a problem that leaves the poorest individuals the most vulnerable to ill climate outcomes, while the poorest people are also the ones least equipt to transition to a low-carbon economy due to issues with economic growth in such areas. This relationship of environment and growth is both reflected in the articulation of problems faced by the global community, as well as shown in the tactics for various projects that the World Bank put forth in the 2006 year. In 2006, the Bank seems to broaden their scope of environmental initiatives. The 2006 report describes various projects that reach beyond the traditional scope of financial lending and grant management projects. For example, the Bank assisted in supporting various legal trials throughout Asia in regards to factory emissions and environmental/health standards. [SEP] Summary Like the 2009 report, the 2010 annual report continued to highlight the importance of moving towards the Millennium Development Goals in the wake of the financial crisis. It also reiternates the sentiment that after the vulnerabilities exposed during the crisis, it is essential to redirect Bank efforts towards greener growth pathways in order to avoid the negative scope of such economic crises in the future. The Bank justifies this reasoning by continuing to assume an interconnectivity between economic health, poverty reduction, and environmental sustainability. This report specifically stresses that a lower-carbon and climate-resilient economic growth path is the best option forward. In 2010, the Bank utilized The International Development Association-- an international financial institution branch of the Bank which offers concessional loans and grants to the world's poorest developing countries-- to address the newly evolving financial and climate action plans needed in wake of the financial crisis. Often the Bank used this mechanism in conjunction with other systems such as the Global Environment Facility to further climate change and carbon-reduction efforts. Additionally, the Bank launched the Pilot Program for Climate Resilience under the CIF’s Strategic Climate Fund in 2010. It also launched the Bank launched the Carbon Partnership Facility (CPF) to create a programmatic approaches for low-carbon growth efforts instead of project-by-project designs. Generally, the Bank expanded its efforts in the climate mitigation realm in 2010, by leveraging a variety of financing instruments, technical assistance, and policy advice to use on projects.

[SEP] OECD Secretary-General’s Report to Ministers 2014 Summary: The OECD’s 2014 Annual Report reiterates themes from recent (past and future) reports regarding environmental sustainability. The Secretary-General’s Strategic Orientation affirm green growth as one of the, if not the, primary goal of the institution. The report goes so far as to say that the green growth framework must “permeate” all levels of the institution and its work. Green growth for the OECD means the creation of coherent policies which promotes economic productivity and environmental sustainability together. The OECD Strategy on Development identifies diminishing multilateral cooperation and stagnant investment as primary obstacles to sustainable development. To correct these failures, the OECD stresses the importance of international and institutional cooperation. The section on the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy lays out general ideas and some specific policy proposals for achieving sustainable and resilient growth. These include investment in technology and infrastructure, effective tax policy (e.g. carbon pricing), subsidy reform, and broader work towards better understanding the synergies between the economy and the environment. The Environment Directorate recognizes the challenges of quantifying the long-term economic impact of environmental degradation and recognizes the need for continued work in this field. The Trade and Agriculture Directorate identifies protectionism and localization as threats to a transition to a green global economy. Multilateralism, investment in R&D (tech, infrastructure), and traditional financial policies are the cornerstone of the OECD’s green growth agenda.

innovation [SEP] Investment and innovation are central to the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy. [SEP] Summary: The 2013 OECD Annual Report outlines the OECD’s commitment to green growth policies. The OECD states that equality and sustainability must be at the center of economic growth, suggesting that while productivity is still key it is no longer the be all end all of growth. The OECD’s Green Growth Strategy claims that not only that “green” and “growth” can go together, but that they must. The OECD asserts that achieving green growth goals must be the result of coordinated international and institutional cooperation. To this end, the OECD attempts to discredit protectionism and suggests that a multilateral approach must be taken to achieve sustainable development goals. Investment and innovation are central to the OECD’s Green Growth Strategy. They also emphasize the need to better understand the long-term economic cost of inaction in the face of environmental crises and, conversely, the long-term economic benefit of positive action. This is as opposed to simply considering short-term costs and benefits which do not fully reflect the consequences of action or inaction. This analysis includes developing new indicators for growth and strengthening our statistical capacities to interpret such data. Green technology and infrastructure are central to a modern green economy. Once environmental assets and natural resources are valued properly, countries will begin to see that it is in their economic interest to protect the environment.

[SEP] OECD Annual Report 2009 Summary: The 2009 OECD Annual Report highlights the need to develop a “cleaner” global economy in the wake of the financial crisis. “Cleaner” has two meanings for the OECD: first, anti-corruption efforts and strengthening corporate governance to create a cleaner globalization and second, fighting environmental degradation and climate change to create a cleaner world. The OECD presents efforts to reduce greenhouse gases as “economically rational”, demonstrating a strong linkage between sustainability and economic development. They further stress that delays in action now will only result in higher costs in the future. The OECD cites investment in eco-innovation as a “win-win” scenario as it leads to the development of environmentally friendly technology while simultaneously acting as a source of growth. To this end, they propose incentivizing R&D in green technology. The report also emphasizes the need to maintain open markets and international trade, arguing that liberalization is the best way to achieve growth and security. The OECD recognizes the need to develop better market tools to help in the pricing of environmental externalities (e.g. carbon tax) as well as restimulating public investment in green R&D. They also propose cap-and-trade as a policy which can identify the cheapest possible abatement opportunities. Goals: “This crisis presents opportunities as well as challenges, and the OECD is seizing these opportunities to formulate policies that will lead to a stronger, cleaner, fairer world economy. over the past year, the OECD has pressed for a “stronger” world economy through its work in areas such as regulation; governance; trade (especially Doha); investment and competition; and, of course, developing policies for sustainable growth. Work on anti-corruption, corporate governance and tax evasion has sought to restore trust in globalisation by making it “cleaner”. so has, literally, our work on environment and climate change, another face of “cleaner”. “Ministers suggested, variously, that future work could analyse and compare concrete national and international policy options to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions from a wide range of activities; analyse incentives for major emitters to take part in international action, including understanding the impacts of climate change on different regions and sectors, and the benefits and co-benefits of action; assess the impact of alternative policies on competitiveness, carbon leakage, financing, technological development and transfer; consider how policies could provide certainty to private investors and remain flexible at the same time; and analyse the economic costs, benefits and distributive aspects of climate change adaptation and mitigation policies.” “OECD work confirms that tackling climate change should not be delayed, and that ambitious action to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is economically rational. The economic crisis provides no room for complacency. at most, it might slightly reduce global emissions temporarily, after which an upward trend will resume. delaying action on climate change would only mean larger cuts later.” “Concerns about the potential carbon leakage and competitiveness impacts of climate policies are often exaggerated. unless only very few countries take action against climate change, carbon leakage rates and competitiveness effects of climate policies are very small … Border tax adjustments or grandfathering domestic emission permits can reduce carbon leakage, but at a cost overall to the economy. If carefully designed, sector-wide agreements covering energy- intensive industries may offer a cheaper and more constructive alternative to mitigate fears of leakage.” “The economic downturn should not weaken efforts to achieve the long-term goal of a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy. The crisis instead presents an opportunity to move towards a stronger, cleaner and fairer world economy. It provides incentives to improve efficiency in the use of energy and materials by getting the prices right, and an opportunity to remove environmentally harmful subsidies, for example, to fossil fuel production and consumption, benefiting both the environment and public budgets.” “Investment in eco-friendly technologies can represent a new source of growth and “win-win” opportunities for both the environment and economic recovery. New low-carbon technologies are key to reducing the future costs of climate change mitigation. stimulus packages could support eco-innovation. examples include offering fiscal incentives for R&D in green technologies.”
